sets.skyview: View from a Kuiper Belt object looking at the sky. Deep-navy starfield with the Milky Way band; the Sun is a small bright white star near the centre, not a disc; four faint dots on a gentle arc near it for Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, tiny cream labels; setp.t 0..1 = slow drift and twinkle; setp.sun 0..1 = the Sun star brightens and a small ring shows its apparent size; setp.labels 0|1 = chips name the dots; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.surface: Surface of a Kuiper Belt object at night. Deep-navy sky with stars and a tiny bright Sun-star low on the horizon; the ground is a dark rounded plain of grey-blue ice with soft frost sparkle and a few low ridges, 4 px outlines, faint cold-cyan rim light; setp.t 0..1 = the camera drifts slowly and frost sparkles; setp.frost 0..1 = frost glints grow; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'.
sets.journey: Route out of the solar system. Deep-navy bg; a small yellow Sun at the left, thin orbit rings for Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune getting wider, then a dotted donut band beyond Neptune; a glowing cyan dotted path runs from Earth out to the band with a small probe dot; setp.t 0..1 = the path draws on and the probe travels; setp.mark 0..1 = a cream ring and tag at the band; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'.
sets.delay: Signal delay diagram. Deep-navy bg; a small blue Earth with a dish on the left, a tiny probe on the right, a long thin cyan line between them with a bright pulse; setp.t 0..1 = the pulse travels from Earth to the probe; setp.back 0..1 = a gold pulse returns; setp.clock 0|1 = a stopwatch face between them shows elapsed hours.
sets.belt: The Kuiper Belt as a thick donut. Deep-navy bg; seen from slightly above: a tiny yellow Sun in the middle, small rings for the planets, Neptune's ring in blue, and a wide fuzzy donut of thousands of tiny pale dots from 30 to 50 AU; setp.t 0..1 = slow camera tilt; setp.edge 0..1 = cream distance ticks 30 AU and 50 AU draw on; setp.scattered 0..1 = a thin cloud of dots stretches far outward; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'.
sets.resonance: Pluto and Neptune orbit dance. Deep-navy bg; a small yellow Sun in the middle, a round blue Neptune orbit and a more oval grey Pluto orbit crossing it, a blue dot and a grey dot circling; setp.t 0..1 = the dots circle (Pluto twice while Neptune goes round three times); setp.count 0..3 = tick marks count the laps; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'.
sets.migrate: Early solar system, the giant planets shifting. Deep-navy bg; a ring of countless tiny icy specks; four large planets in a row (Jupiter big orange, Saturn pale gold, Uranus teal, Neptune blue); setp.t 0..1 = Uranus and Neptune drift outward through the speck ring and specks get flung in curved trails, some inward, some far out; setp.fling 0..1 = most specks are thrown away leaving a thin donut; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'.
sets.arrokoth: Arrokoth close-up. Deep-navy bg; a reddish-brown snowman-shaped object made of two touching lobes, one bigger, 4 px outline, warm rim light on one side, faint craters; setp.t 0..1 = slow rotation; setp.label 0|1 = chips name the two lobes; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.dust: Catching dust high in the sky. Deep-navy-to-pale-blue gradient high-altitude sky with a curved Earth horizon; a sleek twin-tail spy-plane silhouette (ER-2) with a small collector plate under the wing; tiny grey specks drifting; setp.t 0..1 = the plane glides across and specks stick to the plate; setp.zoom 0..1 = camera pushes in to one glowing grain; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'.
sets.isotope: Oxygen isotope lab readout. Deep-navy bg; a big round detector screen, 4 px outline, with two columns of small balls: light oxygen (small, pale) and heavy oxygen (bigger, gold); setp.t 0..1 = the balls fall in; setp.heavy 0..1 = the heavy column fills up past a dashed 'normal' line; setp.ref 0|1 = a second smaller bar labelled GENESIS appears for comparison; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.mass: Mass comparison. Deep-navy bg; a big blue-green Earth ball on the left and a thin pale ring of dots on the right; setp.t 0..1 = the ring thins; setp.now 0..1 = a small bracket marks 10 percent of Earth's mass for the ring today; setp.then 0..1 = a ghost bigger ring shows 7 to 10 Earth masses long ago; setp.glow 'cyan'|'gold'.
sets.scattered: Sedna's long orbit. Deep-navy bg; a tiny Sun far left, Neptune ring, and one very long thin oval orbit stretching to the far right with a small reddish dot (Sedna) on it; cream tick marks for 76 AU and 1,200 AU; setp.t 0..1 = the dot travels along the orbit; setp.ticks 0..1 = the AU marks draw on; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.lab: A bright planetary-science lab. far: wall of dark screens with soft charts and an electron-microscope image; mid: a desk with a microscope, two laptops, a coffee mug and a sticky note; near: carpet GroundPlane with pale rim; setp.alert 0..1 = a screen flashes amber with a magnifier icon; setp.ok 1 = screens turn green.
sets.timeline: A horizontal timeline. Deep-navy bg; a long gold line with milestone dots and cream calendar tags; setp.t 0..1 = the camera pans along the line; setp.now 0..1 = a bright cyan marker glides along and pulses on each dot; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.

props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in hours: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.arrow: Thick outlined curved arrow, pp.color gold|cyan|red, draws on across the shot.
props.flag: Small green check mark badge in a round outlined cream disc with a tiny sparkle; or red cross when pp.bad true.
props.calendar: Small wall calendar page, cream with a red top strip, 4 px outline; pp.text the date in FONTS.title (max 8 chars).
props.magnifier: Outlined magnifying glass with a cream handle and pale glass; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds a cyan bloom in the lens.
props.ring: Pulsing cyan circle outline, 4 px, soft bloom, that expands and fades each second; pp.s scale.
props.scale: Small balance scale icon, cream, 4 px outline, one pan tipped low; pp.s scale; pp.label text beneath.
props.probe: Icon of the BepiColombo stack: a small gold-foil box body with two dark solar-panel wings, a round grey antenna dish and a silver conical sunshield on top, 4 px outline; pp.s scale; pp.glow true adds an orange thruster flame at the bottom.
props.thermo: Tall outlined thermometer, cream glass tube, red or blue fluid to pp.frac (0..1), pp.label text beneath in FONTS.ui; pp.color red|cyan.
props.grain: Tiny dust grain icon: a rough grey-brown speck with a few sparkling facets and a thin pale outline 4 px, on a soft cyan glow; pp.s scale; pp.glow true makes it pulse.

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back (headTilt up), arms hang loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms raised over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation (yaw/spin) across the shot while looking up.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point at the sky at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

chapters.title: THE VIEW
chapters.sub: Where the Sun is a star

film.vo: Four billion miles from the Sun, the Sun is just a star.
Daylight here is a ghost of ours, far too faint to warm you.
NASA just found fresh clues to the ice you'd be standing on.
So what if you stood on a Kuiper Belt world?
Welcome to Ifmosphere. Here are the rules.
The Kuiper Belt is a doughnut of icy leftovers beyond Neptune.
Neptune's orbit marks the inner edge, thirty times Earth's distance.
The main part stretches to about fifty.
Rule one. You land four billion miles out, as in NASA's picture.
Rule two. No radio miracles. Nothing goes faster than light.
Rule three. It's a one way trip.
You wear a plain hooded suit. Keep the hood up.
And here's the catch. The view is the strangest part.
Look up. Find the Sun.
There. That bright pinprick, no bigger than a star.
From here it's forty-three times farther than from Earth.
Light thins out with distance squared, so it's about eighteen hundred times dimmer.
Sunrise, sunset, shadows, all of it, just a bright dot.
Now look around the Sun. Four more dots.
That's Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
NASA's own illustration shows the four largest planets as bright dots.
And the inner planets? Too close to the Sun to see.
Earth, our whole world, is hidden in the Sun's glare.
A Milky Way band arcs over everything, sharp as chalk.
You'd see farther than anyone on Earth ever has.
The ground at your feet glitters faintly with frost.
Remember that ice. NASA scientists just learned something about it.
But first, call home.
Radio travels at the speed of light, and light takes time.
Four billion miles is about twenty-one thousand, five hundred seconds.
That's almost six hours, just for a hello to reach Earth.
And six more hours for anyone to answer.
A twelve hour wait for the reply to hello.
Voyager One just crossed one light-day: twenty-four hours each way.
So you're far, but you're not that far.
Back to the ground. Is anything out here moving?
Astronomers think there are millions of small icy objects out here.
Hundreds of thousands are wider than a hundred kilometres.
But we've catalogued only a little over two thousand.
You are standing in mostly unexplored space.
Time to meet the neighbours.
The king of the Kuiper Belt is Pluto.
Found in nineteen thirty, long before anyone expected a belt.
Pluto orbits twice for every three laps Neptune makes.
Their orbits cross, yet they never meet. A perfect dance.
Pluto even gets closer to Uranus than it ever does to Neptune.
Now a different neighbour. Arrokoth, a snowman.
Two lobes stuck together, red as old rust.
NASA's New Horizons flew past it on the first of January, twenty nineteen.
It's the most distant, most primitive object a spacecraft has ever explored.
Pairs like it may be almost unchanged since birth.
Dwarf planets live here too: Eris, Haumea and Makemake.
Eris, the heaviest of them, drifts in the scattered disk.
And Sedna swings from seventy-six to twelve hundred times Earth's distance.
So how did all this ice end up out here?
Go back to the early solar system.
A thick disk of icy bodies surrounds the young giant planets.
Neptune's gravity stirs it, so the ice can't clump into a planet.
That's the key. Neptune stopped a planet from forming.
Meanwhile Jupiter and Saturn shift, and Uranus and Neptune get pushed outward.
On the way out they plough through the ice like snowploughs.
Jupiter flings most of it into the Oort Cloud, or out entirely.
Today's belt holds no more than about ten percent of Earth's mass.
Once it held seven to ten times Earth's mass.
Most of the belt is already gone.
And what's left is slowly crumbling.
Collisions make smaller bits, and dust that the solar wind blows away.
Dust. Hold that word. It's about to matter.
Eighteen November twenty twenty-six. NASA scientists announce a find.
They studied twelve tiny dust particles.
Not from a spacecraft. From Earth's stratosphere.
NASA's high-altitude research plane scooped them up.
The dust is smaller than a speck, but it carried a secret.
First, where did each grain come from? Tracks of solar particles.
High concentrations of solar energetic particle tracks.
Those tracks trace each grain back to the Kuiper Belt.
Then the minerals. They formed when water touched dust, ages ago.
Researchers used electron microscopy at NASA, and an ion microprobe at UCLA.
The water they found was enriched in heavier oxygen.
Heavier atoms. Same oxygen, but with extra neutrons.
Scientists had suspected ice like that for decades.
Meteorites and asteroid samples hinted at it, but never enough.
Now there's compelling evidence of an ancient reservoir of ice.
A reservoir of ice enriched in heavier oxygen, out in the Kuiper Belt.
NASA's Genesis mission gave scientists a reference to compare against.
Real meteorites rarely show this same signature.
That suggests the giant planets limited mixing between outer and inner solar system.
In other words, a wall of giants kept outer ice outside.
So the ice under your boots is a time capsule.
Chemistry from before the planets finished moving in.
Only a few places keep this record, and you're standing on one.
The scientists say it helps explain how planets formed.
That's a lot of story from twelve grains.
And now you know why the cold open mattered.
Here's the part nobody warns you about. The belt is fading.
The giants threw most of it away, and collisions grind down the rest.
But what remains is the best archive we have.
Pluto, Arrokoth, Eris, Sedna, and millions of unnamed worlds.
Kuiper's paper in nineteen fifty-one guessed at it.
Seventy-five years later, we're reading it in grains of dust.
Remember the cold open. Four billion miles. The Sun, just a star.
Now you know what that dim light was lighting up.
Would you stay a night out here, or run home?
Tomorrow: what if the Moon vanished for one whole day?
Four billion miles out, the Sun is a star, and the ice remembers.

short.vo: Four billion miles out, the Sun is just a star.
short.dir: hushed then hard stop; stress 'just a star'

short.vo: That dot is eighteen hundred times dimmer than our Sun.
Call home, and it takes almost six hours to arrive.
This is the Kuiper Belt, a doughnut of icy leftovers past Neptune.
Hundreds of thousands of worlds wider than a hundred kilometres.
On eighteen November, NASA announced new clues in twelve dust grains.
Their tracks trace back to the Kuiper Belt.
The water inside has extra-heavy oxygen.
Ancient ice, from before the planets stopped moving.
Full film on the channel. Out here, the Sun is just a star.
short.dir: friendly, leading back into the start; stress 'just a star'
